title: Elihu Defends God's Fairness
overview: Elihu, a younger man who has been listening to Job and his friends, argues that God cannot be unjust and accuses Job of speaking against God.

parts.label: A call to weigh words (vv. 1-4)
parts.note: Elihu speaks to the older men listening and asks them to test what they hear the way a tongue tests food. He presents this as working out together what is right, not just announcing it.

parts.label: Elihu's charge against Job (vv. 5-9)
parts.note: He sums up Job's complaint: I am innocent, yet God treats me as guilty and has struck me with an incurable wound. Elihu then says Job is siding with wicked people by claiming it does no good to please God, a conclusion Elihu draws from Job's earlier words rather than a direct quote.

parts.label: God cannot do wrong (vv. 10-15)
parts.note: Elihu insists God repays people for how they live and would never twist justice. His reasoning is that no one handed God the world to manage; it is his own, and every living thing would die if he simply took back his breath.

parts.label: A ruler who judges kings (vv. 16-20)
parts.note: Turning to Job directly, he asks whether someone who hated justice could run the world at all. God treats kings and the poor alike and can remove the powerful suddenly, in the night, with no human hand involved.

parts.label: God sees and acts (vv. 21-30)
parts.note: No darkness can hide wrongdoers from God, so he needs no long trial before he topples oppressors whose victims cried out to him. Even when God seems silent or hidden, Elihu says, no one has grounds to accuse him, and he still keeps the godless from ruling.

parts.label: Elihu's verdict on Job (vv. 31-37)
parts.note: Verses 31 to 33 are hard to translate, but they seem to ask whether Job expects God to deal with him on Job's own terms. Elihu ends by saying Job speaks without understanding, and he wishes Job's testing to go on because Job has added defiance to his wrongdoing.

disagreement: Christians differ on whether Elihu is a wise voice who prepares the way for God's own speech in the following chapters, or another accuser who, like Job's three friends, wrongly assumes Job's suffering must be deserved.
think: When one person insists they have suffered unfairly and another insists the world is run fairly, what would it take for you to be persuaded by either of them?
